choices: The average time miners needed to find the block; used for difficulty.
The time at which the local node first received the block from a peer.
The median timestamp of the 11 preceding blocks; harder for miners to manipulate.
The midpoint between the block's creation and its sixth confirmation.
explanation: getblock shows "the time it was created (according to its miner), the median time of the 11 blocks that precede this block (a time measurement that's harder for miners to manipulate)."

section: Bitcoin Core > Bitcoin Core API > Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface
prompt: What does "RPC" stand for in JSON-RPC, and what transport does Bitcoin Core use for it?
choices: Remote procedure call, carried over HTTP (localhost port 8332 by default).
Rapid payment channel, carried over WebSockets on port 8333.
Replicated peer consensus, carried over the Bitcoin P2P port.
Remote private cache, carried over FTP to the data directory.
explanation: "RPC stands for remote procedure call, which means that we are calling procedures (functions) that are remote (on the Bitcoin Core node) via a network protocol. In this case, the network protocol is HTTP." The curl example connects to 127.0.0.1:8332.

source.book: ch03 > Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface

section: Bitcoin Core > Bitcoin Core API > Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface
prompt: How does Bitcoin Core authenticate RPC clients by default?
choices: The wallet's recovery code must accompany every RPC request.
The node's Bitcoin address is the username and its private key the password.
A random password written to the .cookie file at each start; bitcoin-cli reads it.
No authentication at all; the RPC port accepts requests from anyone.
explanation: "Bitcoin Core will create a random password on each start and place it in the data directory under the name .cookie. The bitcoin-cli helper can read this password file ... you can copy the password and pass it to curl." A static password can be created with share/rpcauth/rpcauth.py.

source.book: ch03 > Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface

section: Bitcoin Core > Bitcoin Core API > Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface
prompt: True or false: The python-bitcoinlib library used in the book's examples is part of the Bitcoin Core project.
explanation: False. "We will use the python-bitcoinlib library to simplify API access. This library is not part of the Bitcoin Core project and needs to be installed the usual way you install Python libraries." It wraps the JSON-RPC API of a running node.

source.book: ch03 > Using Bitcoin Core's Programmatic Interface

section: Bitcoin Core > Bitcoin Core API
prompt: True or false: bitcoin-cli is the Bitcoin node software itself and can validate blocks on its own.
explanation: False. bitcoin-cli is only a command-line helper that sends JSON-RPC requests to a running bitcoind; bitcoind is the daemon that connects to peers, validates blocks, and maintains the blockchain.

section: Bitcoin Core > Full verification nodes (opening)
prompt: In one or two sentences, explain what a full node gives its operator that a lightweight wallet or block explorer cannot.
answer: Independent, authoritative verification: the node checks every confirmed transaction against every consensus rule itself, so the operator need not trust any third party for the validity of the bitcoins they receive and does not reveal which transactions are theirs.
explanation: Key points: self-verification against all rules, no trust in third parties, privacy.

source.book: ch03 > opening; Running a Bitcoin Core Node
source.lecture: W4 s37 +note (full node functions); W4 s29 (miners' UTXO database)

section: Bitcoin Core > Bitcoin Core API > Exploring Blocks
prompt: State the difference between a block's height and its number of confirmations.
answer: Height is the block's position in the chain (how many blocks came before it, genesis being 0); confirmations is its depth (how many blocks have been built on top of it, plus itself), which grows over time and measures how hard it is to reverse.
explanation: Height is fixed; confirmations increase with every new block.

source.lecture: W4 s10-11 +note (blocks every 10 minutes); W4 s51 (6 confirmations)

section: Bitcoin Core > Full node functions (lecture)
prompt: According to the lecture, which functions can a full node perform?
choices: Issuing new bitcoin, setting the exchange rate, and approving new users.
Only relaying transactions; full nodes never store the blockchain.
Wallet, mining, storing and updating a full copy of the blockchain, and network routing for other nodes.
Encrypting the blockchain and decrypting it for paying customers.
explanation: Notes W4 s37: "A node can do all these functions where it can store in a wallet, mine transactions, update/store local blockchain copy, and routing for other nodes. Typically, nodes will do parts of what a full node will do; full nodes are small percentage overall." Notes W4 s38: most miners do not store wallets. The book ch. 1-5 defines a full node by full validation of the entire history; the four-function model is developed in ch10.

source.book: ch01 > Full node versus Lightweight; ch03 > opening

section: Bitcoin Core > Pooled mining (lecture)
prompt: Why, according to the lecture, do almost all miners now mine in pools, and what server supports pooled mining?
choices: Pools are required by the protocol; a Bitcoin Core RPC server coordinates them.
Pools let miners skip transaction validation; an SPV server coordinates them.
The mining difficulty is so high that solo mining rarely succeeds; a Stratum server coordinates the pool.
Pools double the block reward; a Merkle server coordinates them.
explanation: Notes W4 s39: "Typically, miners form a pool since the difficulty of mining is so high now. Almost all are now pool miners." W4 s39 title: "Stratum server: supports pooled mining". The book (ch02): pool miners assign the reward to a pool address and share it in proportion to work contributed.

source.lecture: W4 s39 +note (B22)

section: Bitcoin Core > Exploring the blockchain (lecture close)
prompt: The instructor ended week 4 by pointing students to blockchain explorers. Which statement about explorers is consistent with both the lecture and the book?
choices: Explorers are part of Bitcoin Core and require running a full node.
Explorers can reverse transactions on request.
Explorers show each user's name next to their balance.

Sites such as Blockchair, Blockchain.com, BlockCypher, Blockstream Explorer, and Mempool.Space let you look up addresses, transactions, and blocks; they are third-party web apps, not part of the protocol.
explanation: W4 s56 "Exploring Transactions": Blockchair, Blockchain(.com), Blockcypher; notes: "To end: Explore the blockchain, transactions, etc." W4 s13 also shows blockchair.com. The book (ch02) lists Blockstream Explorer, Mempool.Space, and BlockCypher and warns that looking up your own transactions reveals your interest to the operator; ch03 shows doing the same lookups with your own node via RPC.

source.book: ch02 > Bitcoin Overview (blockchain explorers); ch03 > Bitcoin Core API
source.lecture: W4 s56 +note (E11); W4 s13

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography
prompt: According to the book's sidebar, why does Bitcoin use asymmetric (public/private key) cryptography?
choices: For encrypting each transaction so only the recipient can read the amount.
For compressing the blockchain so full nodes need far less disk space.
For hiding the sender's IP address from the rest of the network.
For digital signatures that anyone can verify, not for encrypting transactions.
explanation: "It's not used to 'encrypt' (make secret) the transactions. Rather, a useful property of asymmetric cryptography is the ability to generate digital signatures ... anyone can verify every signature on every transaction, while ensuring that only the owners of private keys can produce valid signatures."

source.lecture: W2 s18-20 +note ('bitcoin does not directly encrypt messages'); W2 s24-25 +note ('Encryption is not used directly in bitcoin/blockchain but does use the public key digital signature')

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography
prompt: In a Bitcoin key pair, which key is used to receive funds and which to spend them?
choices: The private key receives funds; the public key signs to spend them.
Both keys must be revealed to the payer before funds can be received.
The public key spends funds; the private key serves only as a backup.
The public key receives funds; the private key signs to spend them.
explanation: "The public key is used to receive funds, and the private key is used to sign transactions to spend the funds." Signatures can be validated against the public key without revealing the private key.

source.lecture: W4 s7 +note (sign with secret key Ks, verify with public key Kp); W4 s9 +note (receive to Hash(Kp), spend by signing)

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Private Keys
prompt: What is a Bitcoin private key, at its most basic?
choices: A password chosen by the user and registered with the network.
A key file issued by Bitcoin Core when the wallet is first installed.
The SHA256 hash of the user's Bitcoin address, computed by the wallet.
Simply a random 256-bit number, usually shown as 64 hex digits.
explanation: "A private key is simply a number, picked at random." The TIP notes you could generate one by tossing a coin 256 times. It is not chosen by the user, not issued by anyone, and not derived from the address (derivation runs the other way).

source.lecture: W2 s80 +note (select d at random, compute Q = dG); W4 s9 +note ('Generate a random pair of public/secret keys')

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Private Keys
prompt: What happens if a Bitcoin private key is lost, and what happens if it is revealed to someone else?
choices: If lost, the network can reissue it after identity verification; if revealed, nothing happens because the public key is still secret.
If lost, it cannot be recovered and the funds it secures are lost forever; if revealed, the other party gains full control of those funds.
If lost, the funds return to the miners; if revealed, the funds are frozen.
Neither matters because the wallet's recovery code is stored on the blockchain.
explanation: "The private key must remain secret at all times because revealing it to third parties is equivalent to giving them control over the bitcoins secured by that key. The private key must also be backed up ... because if it's lost, it cannot be recovered and the funds secured by it are forever lost too."

source.lecture: W4 s9 +note ('Alice is the only party with the secret key'); W4 s6 Q1-Q3

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Private Keys
prompt: What does the book say is the first and most important step in generating keys?
choices: Obtaining secure randomness (entropy) from a CSPRNG.
Registering the newly created key with a full node.
Choosing a memorable passphrase to protect the key.
Selecting which elliptic curve the key will use.
explanation: "The first and most important step in generating keys is to find a secure source of randomness (which computer scientists call entropy)." The WARNING adds: do not write your own random number generator or use a 'simple' RNG; use a CSPRNG. The curve is fixed (secp256k1).

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Elliptic Curve Cryptography Explained
prompt: Which elliptic curve does Bitcoin use for its keys?
choices: Curve25519, whose equation is y^2 = x^3 + 486662x^2 + x.
NIST P-256 (secp256r1), a random-parameter curve.
secp256k1, whose equation is y^2 = x^3 + 7.
The RSA-2048 curve, based on a 2,048-bit modulus.
explanation: "Bitcoin uses a specific elliptic curve and set of mathematical constants, as defined in a standard called secp256k1 ... defined by the following function ... y^2 = (x^3 + 7) over F_p." RSA is not an elliptic-curve system at all.

source.lecture: W2 s79 +note ('in Bitcoin, we use secp256k1 ... a Koblitz curve'; y^2 = x^3 + 7 mod p; same p formula as the book)

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Elliptic Curve Cryptography Explained
prompt: Elliptic curve cryptography, as described in the book, derives its security from which hard problem?
choices: The problem of factoring the product of two large prime numbers.
The discrete logarithm problem on the points of an elliptic curve.
The problem of finding two inputs that collide under SHA256.
The traveling salesman problem over the curve's points.
explanation: "Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) is a type of asymmetric or public key cryptography based on the discrete logarithm problem as expressed by addition and multiplication on the points of an elliptic curve." Factoring underlies RSA, not ECC.

source.lecture: W2 s41-42 +note (discrete logarithm infeasible); W2 s62 (why EC: 160-bit EC ~ 1024-bit traditional)

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Public Keys
prompt: How is a Bitcoin public key derived from a private key?
choices: By hashing the private key with SHA256 and then RIPEMD-160.
By encrypting the private key with the wallet's passphrase.
By base58check-encoding the private key with a version byte.
By elliptic-curve multiplication: K = k x G, with G a fixed generator point.
explanation: "The public key is calculated from the private key using elliptic curve multiplication, which is irreversible: K = k x G, where k is the private key, G is a constant point called the generator point, and K is the resulting public key." Hashing comes later, when making an address.

source.lecture: W2 s80 +note (Q = d*G with base point G) - lecture writes d/Q where the book writes k/K

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Public Keys
prompt: Why can a Bitcoin public key be shared freely without revealing the private key?
choices: The public key is stored encrypted under the wallet's password.
The network erases the private key once the public key is generated.
The public key is only 33 bytes, too short to reveal a 32-byte key.
Elliptic-curve multiplication is one-way; recovering k from K is infeasible.
explanation: "Elliptic curve multiplication is a type of function that cryptographers call a 'trap door' function: it is easy to do in one direction (multiplication) and impossible to do in the reverse direction (division) ... no one can reverse the function and calculate the private key from the public key."

source.lecture: W2 s5 +note (one-wayness: 'theoretically you can but practically you cannot reverse'); W2 s41-42 +note (discrete log)

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Public Keys
prompt: True or false: Given enough time, a Bitcoin public key can be converted back into its private key because the math works in both directions.
explanation: False. "A private key can be converted into a public key, but a public key cannot be converted back into a private key because the math only works one way." Recovering k from K = kG is the discrete logarithm problem, considered infeasible.

source.lecture: W2 s41-42 +note ('calculating the x ... infeasible'); W2 s80

section: Keys and Addresses > Output and Input Scripts
prompt: How does the book summarize the roles of output scripts and input scripts?
choices: Output scripts act like public keys; input scripts act like signatures.
Output scripts hold the private key; input scripts hold the block hash.
Output scripts are used only by miners; input scripts only by wallets.
Output scripts encrypt the amount; input scripts decrypt it for spending.
explanation: "For now, all we need to understand is that bitcoins are received to an output script that acts like a public key, and bitcoin spending is authorized by an input script that acts like a signature." These fields allow extra conditions beyond a simple signature check.

source.lecture: W4 s27-28 (slide: ScriptSig 'typically signature + public key', scriptPubKey 'public key script'); W4 s30 (P2PKH script bytes)

section: Keys and Addresses > IP Addresses: The Original Address for Bitcoin (P2PK)
prompt: In Bitcoin 0.1, what could a spender enter instead of a public key to pay someone, and why was this feature removed?
choices: The receiver's email address; it was dropped because email is insecure.
The receiver's bank account number; it was dropped for regulatory reasons.
The receiver's IP address; it required the receiver to be online and reachable.
The receiver's phone number; it was dropped once smartphones appeared.
explanation: "The earliest version of Bitcoin software allowed a spender to enter the receiver's IP address ... This feature was later removed--there are many problems with using IP addresses." A key downside: "the receiver needs their wallet to be online at their IP address, and it needs to be accessible from the outside world."

source.book: ch04 > IP Addresses: The Original Address for Bitcoin (P2PK)

section: Keys and Addresses > IP Addresses: The Original Address for Bitcoin (P2PK)
prompt: What is a P2PK (pay to public key) output, and how widely was it used?
choices: A payment to a hash of the public key; still the most common type today.
An output requiring two signatures; used for all exchange withdrawals.
An output with no script at all; it was banned in the 2017 upgrade.
<public key> OP_CHECKSIG, spent with just a signature; never widely used.
explanation: "Alice's wallet would construct a transaction output paying a very simple output script: <Bob's public key> OP_CHECKSIG. Bob would later be able to spend that output with an input script consisting entirely of his signature ... This type of output is known today as pay to public key, or P2PK for short. It was never widely used for payments."

source.book: ch04 > IP Addresses: The Original Address for Bitcoin (P2PK)

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH
prompt: Why does the book describe the output of a secure hash function as a "commitment"?
choices: The hash can be decrypted later to reveal the input it was made from.
Miners must commit to paying a fee for every hash they publish.
The hash is countersigned by a trusted authority before use.
Same input always gives that output, and no other input feasibly does.
explanation: "A cryptographic hash function will always produce the same output when given the same input, and a secure function will also make it impractical for somebody to choose a different input that produces a previously-seen output. That makes the output a commitment to the input." The book's example commits to the answer '2007' for when Satoshi started work.

source.lecture: W2 s5-9 +note (one-wayness, collision resistance, random oracle: 'any bit swapped makes the output completely different'); W4 s17 +note

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH
prompt: How does the original Bitcoin software create the 20-byte commitment to a public key used in P2PKH?
choices: SHA256 applied twice to the public key, then truncated to 20 bytes.
The first 20 bytes of the public key, with the rest discarded.
SHA256 first, then RIPEMD-160 on the result: RIPEMD160(SHA256(K)).
The public key encrypted under the corresponding private key.
explanation: "The original version of Bitcoin made commitments to public keys by first hashing the key with SHA256 and then hashing that output with RIPEMD-160; this produced a 20-byte commitment to the public key." SHA256 alone gives 32 bytes; RIPEMD-160 gives 160 bits = 20 bytes. This combination is known as HASH160.

source.lecture: W4 s9 +note ('Account # = Hash(Kp)'); W4 s30 (slide: OP_HASH160 + 20-byte PubKey hash) - the SHA256+RIPEMD-160 detail is book-only

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH
prompt: Which output script is the P2PKH template described in the book?
choices: OP_HASH160 <commitment> OP_EQUAL (spent with a redeem script)
<public key> OP_CHECKSIG (spent with a bare signature only)
OP_0 <20-byte witness program> (spent with witness data)
OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <commitment> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG
explanation: The P2PKH walk-through: OP_DUP duplicates the pubkey, OP_HASH160 hashes the copy, the commitment is pushed, OP_EQUALVERIFY checks they match, and OP_CHECKSIG verifies the signature. The other templates are P2SH, P2PK, and P2WPKH respectively.

source.lecture: W4 s30-31 (slide only: scriptPubKey 'OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG')

section: Keys and Addresses > Base58check Encoding
prompt: Which characters does base58 omit compared with base64, and why?
choices: 0, O, l, I and the symbols + and /, because they are easily confused.
All vowels, to prevent addresses from spelling offensive words.
All digits, so that addresses consist only of letters.
The letters x, y, and z, which are reserved for extended keys.
explanation: "Base58 is base64 without the 0 (number zero), O (capital o), l (lower L), I (capital i), and the symbols '+' and '/'." The result is the 58-character alphabet 123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz.

section: Keys and Addresses > Base58check Encoding
prompt: What does the "check" in base58check add, and how is it computed?
choices: A 4-byte checksum: the first four bytes of a double SHA256 of the data.
A digital signature over the address made by the wallet developer.
A 20-byte RIPEMD-160 hash of the address appended to the end.
A parity bit appended after each character of the address.
explanation: "To add extra security against typos or transcription errors, base58check includes a checksum ... an additional four bytes added to the end of the data ... we compute the 'double-SHA' checksum ... From the resulting 32-byte hash (hash-of-a-hash), we take only the first four bytes." A mismatch means the address is invalid, preventing loss of funds.

section: Keys and Addresses > Base58check Encoding
prompt: What is the purpose of the version byte prepended before base58check encoding?
choices: It records which Bitcoin Core release generated the key.
It stores the fee rate the wallet intends to pay when spending.
It identifies the data type and sets the leading character (1, 3, 5, xpub...).
It indicates how many confirmations payments to the address have.
explanation: "We first add a prefix to the data, called the 'version byte,' which serves to easily identify the type of data that is encoded ... These characters make it easy for humans to identify the type of data that is encoded and how to use it." Other examples: 0x80 -> WIF private keys starting with 5/K/L; 0x0488B21E -> xpub.

section: Keys and Addresses > Base58check Encoding
prompt: A mainnet Bitcoin address begins with the character "3". What does that tell you?
choices: A legacy pay-to-public-key-hash (P2PKH) address, version byte 0x00.
A legacy pay-to-script-hash (P2SH) address, version byte 0x05.
A testnet address, since mainnet addresses never start with 3.
A segwit address encoded with bech32 rather than base58check.
explanation: From the version-prefix table: P2PKH addresses (0x00) start with 1; P2SH addresses (0x05) start with 3; testnet P2PKH starts with m or n and testnet P2SH with 2; bech32 addresses start with bc1.

source.book: ch04 > Base58check Encoding; Legacy Pay to Script Hash

section: Keys and Addresses > Compressed Public Keys
prompt: What is a compressed public key, and why is it possible?
choices: A public key passed through a zip algorithm to save storage space.
33 bytes: prefix 02/03 (y's parity) plus x, since y is recoverable from x.
A public key truncated to its first 33 bytes at some cost to security.
A public key whose y coordinate is encrypted under the private key.
explanation: "If we know the x coordinate, we can calculate the y coordinate by solving the equation ... That allows us to store only the x coordinate of the public key point, omitting the y coordinate and reducing the size of the key ... by 256 bits." The 02/03 prefix records whether y is even or odd; uncompressed keys use prefix 04 and are 65 bytes.

section: Keys and Addresses > Compressed Public Keys
prompt: The same private key is used to produce a compressed and an uncompressed public key. What does the book say about the resulting addresses?
choices: The same address, because an address depends only on the private key.
Only the uncompressed key yields a valid address; the other is rejected.
The compressed key yields a testnet address instead of a mainnet one.
Two different addresses, because the two encodings hash differently.
explanation: "If we convert this compressed public key to a commitment using the HASH160 function, it will produce a different commitment than the uncompressed public key, leading to a different address ... a single private key can produce a public key expressed in two different formats (compressed and uncompressed) that produce two different Bitcoin addresses."

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH)
prompt: What did BIP16 (2012) introduce, and what does the output script commit to?
choices: Pay to script hash: OP_HASH160 <hash> OP_EQUAL commits to a redeem script.
Segregated witness: OP_0 <program> commits to a witness program.
Compressed public keys: prefix 02/03 commits to the x coordinate.
Bech32 addresses: a six-character BCH checksum commits to the data.
explanation: "The BIP16 upgrade to the Bitcoin protocol in 2012 allows an output script to commit to a redemption script (redeem script). When Bob spends his bitcoins, his input script needs to provide a redeem script that matches the commitment and also any data necessary to satisfy the redeem script." Segwit came in 2017.

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH)

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH)
prompt: True or false: A P2SH address (starting with 3) always represents a multisignature script.
explanation: False. "P2SH is not necessarily the same as a multisignature transaction. A P2SH address most often represents a multisignature script, but it might also represent a script encoding other types of transactions."

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH) (TIP)
source.lecture: W2 s47-48 +note (multi-signatures: 'multiple parties have to participate'); P2SH itself is book-only

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH)
prompt: Which two script templates are the only ones encoded with base58check, and what are they collectively called today?
choices: P2PKH and P2SH, now called legacy addresses.
P2PK and P2TR, now called witness addresses.
P2WPKH and P2WSH, now called segwit addresses.
P2SH and P2TR, now called taproot addresses.
explanation: "P2PKH and P2SH are the only two script templates used with base58check encoding. They are now known as legacy addresses and have become less common over time. Legacy addresses were supplanted by the bech32 family of addresses."

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH)

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Pay to Script Hash (P2SH)
prompt: Why does the book say a 160-bit hash such as HASH160 can be vulnerable to a collision attack when multiple parties build a P2SH multisig address?
choices: RIPEMD-160 is fully broken, so any desired output can be forged instantly.
Multisig redeem scripts are stored in the clear and never hashed at all.
The base58check checksum is only four bytes, so addresses collide often.
An attacker who can influence the input cuts the strength to about 2^80.
explanation: "When an attacker is able to influence the original input value ... the strength of hash algorithm is reduced to its square root. For HASH160, the probability becomes 1-in-2^80. This is a collision attack." All Bitcoin miners perform about 2^80 hashes per hour, so the book recommends newer address types with at least 128 bits of collision resistance.

source.lecture: W2 s6 +note (two types of collision); W2 s11-16 +note (birthday attack; brute force ~2^(n/2))

section: Keys and Addresses > Bech32 Addresses
prompt: What did the 2017 segregated witness (segwit) upgrade accomplish, according to the chapter?
choices: Replaced proof of work with proof of stake to cut electricity use.
Removed the 21 million coin limit to allow continued issuance.
Fixed third-party txid malleability, added capacity, and enabled new outputs.
Encrypted transaction amounts to make all payments private.
explanation: "In 2017, the Bitcoin protocol was upgraded. When the upgrade is used, it prevents transaction identifiers (txids) from being changed without the consent of a spending user ... The upgrade, called segregated witness (or segwit for short), also provided additional capacity for transaction data in blocks and several other benefits."

source.lecture: W2 s82 +note (ECDSA malleability 'one of the root causes of Bitcoin transaction malleability'); W2 s84 (EC-Schnorr free of malleability)

section: Keys and Addresses > Bech32 Addresses
prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the problems with base58check that motivated bech32?
choices: Base58check addresses cannot encode private keys.
Its mixed-case alphabet is inconvenient to read aloud or transcribe.
It can detect errors but cannot help the user locate or correct them.
Its mixed-case alphabet requires more space in QR codes.
explanation: The book lists four problems: mixed case is hard to read/transcribe, errors are detected but not located, QR codes must be larger, and every spender wallet must upgrade for each new feature. Base58check does encode private keys (WIF), so that is not a problem it has.

section: Keys and Addresses > Bech32 Addresses
prompt: Which error-detection property does the book attribute to bech32 addresses of the expected length?
choices: Automatic and silent correction of any number of transcription errors.
Detection limited to errors in the first character of the address.
Guaranteed detection of any error affecting up to four characters, plus location.
No error detection at all; wallets must query a server to validate.
explanation: "In an address of an expected length, it is mathematically guaranteed to detect any error affecting four characters or less; that's more reliable than base58check ... for an address typed with just a few errors, it can tell the user where those errors occurred." The book also stresses using the checksum for detection only, not automatic correction.

section: Keys and Addresses > Bech32 Addresses > Bech32m
prompt: Two Bitcoin addresses start with "bc1q" and "bc1p" respectively. What does the character after "bc1" indicate?
choices: The network: q marks a mainnet address and p marks a testnet address.
The segwit version: q is version 0 (bech32), p is version 1, taproot (bech32m).
The key type: q marks a compressed and p an uncompressed public key.
The checksum: q means SHA256 was used and p means RIPEMD-160.
explanation: "The letter 'q' is the encoding of '0' for segwit v0, the initial version of segwit where bech32 addresses were introduced. The letter 'p' is the encoding of '1' for segwit v1 (also called taproot) where bech32m began to be used." The network is indicated by the HRP (bc mainnet, tb testnet).

source.lecture: W4 s46, s49-50 (skipped case study: Feds address bc1q... = pay-to-witness-pubkey-hash vs 1HQ3... = pay-to-pubkey-hash)

section: Keys and Addresses > Bech32 Addresses > Bech32m
prompt: In a bech32/bech32m address such as bc1q..., what are the "bc" and the "1"?
choices: bc is the HRP (mainnet; tb = testnet) and 1 is a separator, not data.
bc abbreviates 'base checksum' and 1 is the address version number.
bc is the first two bytes of the public key and 1 means one signature.
bc identifies Bitcoin Core wallets and 1 means one confirmation so far.
explanation: "Bech32m addresses start with a human readable part (HRP) ... bc = Bitcoin mainnet, tb = Bitcoin testnet. The HRP is followed by a separator, the number '1.'" A number was chosen so double-click selection works, and '1' because it is not otherwise used in the alphabet (avoiding confusion with 'l').

section: Keys and Addresses > Bech32 Addresses > Bech32m
prompt: What is bech32m and why was it created?
choices: A bech32 variant designed for mobile wallets, using a shorter 16-character alphabet.
Bech32 with one checksum constant changed to catch insertions/deletions; for v1+.
A bech32 variant that reuses the base58 alphabet for backward compatibility.
An entirely new address format that replaces every existing bc1q address.
explanation: "Developers exhaustively analyzed the bech32 problem and found that changing a single constant in their algorithm would eliminate the problem ... The version of bech32 with a single different constant is known as bech32 modified (bech32m)." bech32 remains in use for segwit v0 (bc1q); bech32m addresses differ only in the last six characters.

section: Keys and Addresses > Private Key Formats / Compressed Private Keys
prompt: A private key is exported in Wallet Import Format (WIF). What are its characteristics?
choices: Plain hexadecimal with no checksum, always exactly 64 characters.
Bech32 with the human-readable part bc, starting with bc1.
Base58check with version 0x80, starting with 5 (K/L if compressed).
A 12-word phrase drawn from the BIP39 word list.
explanation: The private-key format table: Hex (64 digits, no prefix), WIF (prefix 5; base58check with version 128 and a 32-bit checksum), WIF-compressed (prefix K or L; suffix 0x01 added before encoding). WIF is used for import/export between wallets and in QR codes.

section: Keys and Addresses > Private Key Formats / Compressed Private Keys
prompt: Why does the book call the term "compressed private key" a misnomer?
choices: Compressed private keys are 16 bytes long instead of the usual 32.
Compression weakens the key, so the name understates the risk.
Only hardware wallets can decompress them back to a usable key.
Nothing is compressed; WIF-compressed is one byte longer and only flags pubkey type.
explanation: "The commonly used term 'compressed private key' is a misnomer, because when a private key is exported as WIF-compressed, it is actually one byte longer than an 'uncompressed' private key ... Private keys are not themselves compressed and cannot be compressed." The extra byte changes the leading base58 character from 5 to K or L.

section: Keys and Addresses > Advanced Keys and Addresses (Vanity, Paper Wallets)
prompt: How secure is a vanity address (e.g., one starting with 1Kids) compared with an ordinary address?
choices: Less secure, because the predictable prefix narrows the key search.
Equally secure; it uses the same curve and hash functions as any address.
More secure, because far more computation went into creating it.
Insecure, because the chosen pattern leaks bits of the private key.
explanation: "Vanity addresses are no less or more secure than any other address. They depend on the same elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) and secure hash algorithm (SHA) as any other address. You can no more easily find the private key of an address starting with a vanity pattern than you can any other address."

section: Keys and Addresses > Advanced Keys and Addresses (Vanity, Paper Wallets)
prompt: Why have vanity addresses almost entirely disappeared from use, according to the book?
choices: A 2017 protocol change made vanity patterns invalid in new addresses.
Each display of a vanity address now incurs a transaction fee.
GPUs became too slow to find patterns of more than three characters.
Deterministic wallets can't import them, and reuse links payments (privacy).
explanation: The book gives two causes: deterministic wallets ("most wallets using deterministic key generation simply don't allow importing a private key or key tweak from a vanity generator") and avoiding address reuse ("using a vanity address to receive multiple payments to the same address creates a link between all of those payments").

source.book: ch04 > Vanity address security and privacy

section: Keys and Addresses > Advanced Keys and Addresses (Vanity, Paper Wallets)
prompt: What is the book's verdict on paper wallets?
choices: The recommended way to store large amounts of bitcoin for the long term.
Safe as long as the paper is laminated and stored in a fireproof safe.
Obsolete and dangerous; use a recovery code (and a hardware signer) instead.
Required by most exchanges before they will send a withdrawal.
explanation: The WARNING: "Paper wallets are an OBSOLETE technology and are dangerous for most users ... Many bitcoins have been stolen this way ... Use a recovery code to back up your keys, possibly with a hardware signing device to store keys and sign transactions. DO NOT USE PAPER WALLETS."

section: Keys and Addresses > Base58check Encoding
prompt: True or false: A legacy Bitcoin address is simply the public key encoded in base58.
explanation: False. A legacy address is the base58check encoding of a version byte plus a 20-byte HASH160 commitment (hash) of the public key (or of a redeem script for P2SH) plus a 4-byte checksum; the public key itself is revealed only when the output is spent.

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH; Base58check Encoding
source.lecture: W4 s9 +note ('digital signature - ties Alice to the account using a hash of the public key')

section: Keys and Addresses > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH
prompt: Describe the steps that turn a public key into a legacy (P2PKH) Bitcoin address.
answer: Hash the public key with SHA256, then hash that result with RIPEMD-160 to get a 20-byte commitment (HASH160); prepend the version byte 0x00; compute a 4-byte checksum as the first four bytes of SHA256(SHA256(version||hash)); append it; encode the whole thing in base58, yielding an address that starts with 1.
explanation: Key points: SHA256 then RIPEMD-160; version byte; double-SHA256 checksum (4 bytes); base58; leading 1.

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH; Base58check Encoding
source.lecture: W4 s9 +note (Account # = Hash(Kp)); W4 s30 (OP_HASH160, 20-byte hash)

section: Keys and Addresses > Public Key Cryptography > Public Keys
prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why sharing a Bitcoin public key or address does not endanger the funds it controls.
answer: The public key is derived from the private key by elliptic-curve multiplication (K = k x G), a one-way function whose reversal is the intractable discrete logarithm problem; an address is additionally only a hash of the key. Spending requires a signature that only the private key can produce, so knowing K or the address gives no ability to spend.
explanation: Key points: one-way derivation; discrete log infeasible; signatures need the private key.

source.lecture: W2 s5 +note; W2 s41-42 +note; W4 s9 +note

section: Keys and Addresses > Cryptographic foundations (lecture week 2)
prompt: Which three basic cryptographic algorithms did the week-2 lecture name as the foundations of cryptocurrencies?
choices: One-way hash algorithms, public key digital signatures, and elliptic curve cryptography.
Symmetric encryption, password hashing, and steganography.
RSA encryption, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and AES.
Merkle trees, Bloom filters, and zero-knowledge proofs.
explanation: W2 s2 "Basic Cryptographic Algorithms": one-way hash algorithm; public key digital signature; elliptic curve cryptography. Mastering Bitcoin ch04 uses all three: hash functions as commitments, signatures to authorize spending, and secp256k1 elliptic-curve keys.

source.book: ch04 > Public Key Cryptography; Legacy Addresses for P2PKH (hash functions)
source.lecture: W2 s2 +note

section: Keys and Addresses > Digital signature properties (lecture)
prompt: Which set of properties of digital signatures did the week-2 lecture list?
choices: Secret, reversible, recognizable by handwriting experts, and identical for every document.
Encrypted, revocable by the recipient, verifiable only by banks, and reusable across documents.
Unforgeable, undeniable by the signer (non-repudiation), universally verifiable, and different from document to document.
Anonymous, transferable, valid for 10 minutes, and issued by miners.
explanation: W2 s26 "Useful Properties of Digital Signature": unforgeable ("takes 1 billion years to forge"), un-deniable by the signatory, universally verifiable, differs from document to document, easily implementable. Notes W2 s26-27: changing the amount on the signed bill invalidates the signature. The book: anyone can verify every signature while only private-key holders can produce them.

source.book: ch04 > Public Key Cryptography (sidebar on digital signatures)
source.lecture: W2 s26-27 +note

section: Keys and Addresses > One-way hash properties (lecture)
prompt: Which statement matches the lecture's definition of a one-way hash algorithm?
choices: It encrypts an input so that only the key holder can recover it.
It maps a fixed-length input to a variable-length output that grows with security.

It maps an input of any length (even an empty string) to a fixed-length output (e.g., 256 bits); it is infeasible to find an input for a given output (one-wayness) or two inputs with the same output (collision resistance).
It compresses a file so that the original can be perfectly reconstructed.
explanation: W2 s4-5: a document of any length -> condensed output of fixed length (say 256 bits / 32 bytes); one-wayness; collision resistance. Notes W2 s4: "Input can be any length, even an empty string; key difference between one-way hash function and others." W2 s9: deterministic yet random-oracle-like. The book (ch04): a hash function takes a potentially large input and outputs a fixed amount of data; the output is a commitment.

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH (hash functions and commitments)
source.lecture: W2 s4-9 +note (E5, E6)

section: Keys and Addresses > Collision types and the birthday attack (lecture)
prompt: The lecture distinguished two types of hash collision and explained the birthday attack. Which statement is correct?
choices: Type 1: given a specific input, find a different input with the same hash; Type 2: find any two inputs that collide. The birthday paradox makes Type 2 roughly as hard as 2^(n/2) trials for an n-bit hash, not 2^n.
Both types are equally hard and require 2^n trials for an n-bit hash.
Type 1 is impossible in principle; Type 2 requires knowing the private key.
Collisions can only be found by decrypting the hash.
explanation: W2 s6 "2 Types of Collision"; W2 s11-16: brute force uses the birthday paradox (23 people give a 50% chance of a shared birthday, 57 give 99%); SHA-256's birthday bound is 2^128. The book's P2SH collision sidebar (ch04) makes the same point: a 160-bit hash gives only 2^80 collision resistance when the attacker can influence the input.

source.lecture: W2 s6, s11-16 +note (S7)

section: Keys and Addresses > SHA family (lecture)
prompt: Which statement about the SHA hash families matches the week-2 lecture?
choices: SHA-1 is the strongest because it is the oldest and most tested.
SHA-256 was broken in 2015 and replaced by MD5.
SHA-1 (1995) is no longer secure; SHA-2 (2001), including SHA-256, and SHA-3 (2015) are still considered secure.
SHA-3 is the only family Bitcoin can use.
explanation: W2 s10 table: SHA1 (SHA-160, 1995) still secure? No; SHA2 (SHA-224/256/384/512, 2001) Yes; SHA3 (2015) Yes. Notes W2 s10: "SHA2 is still a strong standard for security though it was conservatively produced in 2001." Bitcoin uses SHA-256 (the book, ch04) and RIPEMD-160.

source.lecture: W2 s10, s16 +note

section: Keys and Addresses > secp256k1 parameters (lecture)
prompt: The lecture called Bitcoin's curve a "Koblitz curve" and listed system-wide parameters shared by all parties. Which parameter set is correct?
choices: (N, e, d): an RSA modulus with public and private exponents.
(p, q, g, y): the DSS public key parameters.
(E, G, p, n): the curve E (y^2 = x^3 + 7 over GF(p)), a base point G, the prime p, and the (prime) order n of the group of points.
(k, r, s): a private key and a signature pair.
explanation: W2 s79: "(E, G, p, n) are system-wide parameters, used by all parties in Bitcoin ... The elliptic curve E (a Koblitz curve): y^2 = x^3 + 7 mod p"; notes W2 s79: "in the case of bitcoin, a Koblitz curve was selected." The book (ch04) gives the same equation, p = 2^256 - 2^32 - 2^9 - 2^8 - 2^7 - 2^6 - 2^4 - 1, and the generator point G, but never uses the word Koblitz. (N, e, d) is RSA; (p, q, g, y) is DSS.

source.book: ch04 > Elliptic Curve Cryptography Explained; Public Keys (generator point)
source.lecture: W2 s79 +note (B6)

section: Keys and Addresses > ECDSA malleability (lecture)
prompt: What is the "twin signature" problem of ECDSA that the lecture linked to Bitcoin transaction malleability?
choices: Any two users who pick the same private key produce identical signatures.
ECDSA signatures can be reused on any other message from the same signer.

If (r, s) is a valid signature, then (r, -s mod n), i.e., (r, n - s), is also valid, because r depends only on the x-coordinate of kG; a third party can swap in the twin and change the transaction's ID.
The public key can be recovered from a signature, revealing the private key.
explanation: W2 s82: "If (r, s) is a valid signature of m, then both (r, -s mod n) and (r, n - s) are a valid signature of m also ... This is one of the root causes of Bitcoin 'transaction malleability'." Notes W2 s82: the twin lets someone "replace the original signature with the digital twin" producing a different but valid transaction. The book: a txid is not authoritative before confirmation (ch03) and segwit (2017) prevents third-party txid changes (ch04).

source.book: ch03 > Exploring and Decoding Transactions (malleability TIP); ch04 > Bech32 Addresses (segwit fixes malleability)
source.lecture: W2 s82 +note (B7)

section: Keys and Addresses > Schnorr vs ECDSA (lecture)
prompt: According to the lecture, why is EC-Schnorr considered better than ECDSA, and how does it relate to Bitcoin?
choices: It uses shorter private keys, so wallets need less storage; Bitcoin has never used it.
It encrypts the transaction as well as signing it; Bitcoin uses it for all private payments.

It admits security proofs, supports threshold/multi-signatures (MuSig) and blind signatures, is free of signature malleability, and is cleaner and slightly faster; the instructor said Bitcoin has adopted the Schnorr (r, s) approach.
It requires no random number, so it can run without entropy; Bitcoin banned it in 2017.
explanation: W2 s84 "Why EC-Schnorr is better?": security proofs, easy threshold signature, blind signature, free of signature malleability, cleaner and slightly faster. Notes W2 s46: "Bitcoin has moved to the 'r, s version'"; notes W2 s85: "the EC-Schnorr Multi-Signature approach is what is actually used by bitcoin." Book context (ch04): taproot (segwit v1, bc1p... addresses) is the output type that uses Schnorr signatures; legacy and segwit v0 outputs still use ECDSA.

section: Keys and Addresses > Hard problems behind signatures (lecture)
prompt: Which "hard problem" underlies RSA, and which underlies the elliptic-curve signatures Bitcoin uses?
choices: RSA rests on the difficulty of factoring the product of two large primes; DSS, Schnorr, and elliptic-curve schemes rest on the discrete logarithm problem.
RSA rests on the discrete logarithm problem; elliptic-curve schemes rest on factoring.
Both rest on the difficulty of finding hash collisions.
RSA rests on the traveling salesman problem; elliptic-curve schemes rest on graph coloring.
explanation: Notes W2 s33: RSA is secure because of the "factorization problem"; W2 s28: DSS and Schnorr are "based on infeasibility of discrete logarithm"; W2 s41-42 and s61-62: discrete logs in finite fields and on elliptic curves. The book (ch04): ECC is based on the discrete logarithm problem; prime-number exponentiation and elliptic-curve multiplication are both one-way functions.

source.book: ch04 > Public Key Cryptography; Elliptic Curve Cryptography Explained

section: Keys and Addresses > Post-quantum cryptography (lecture)
prompt: True or false: According to the lecture, RSA, DSS, Schnorr, and elliptic-curve signatures can all be broken by sufficiently powerful quantum computers, motivating post-quantum signature standards such as Dilithium and SPHINCS+.
explanation: True. Notes W2 s28: "RSA, DSS, Schnorr digital signature, and elliptic curves can all be broken by quantum computers. People are trying to build post-quantum secure blockchains." W2 s28 and s100 name Dilithium (module-lattice) and SPHINCS+ (stateless hash-based); notes W2 s100 add that Ethereum is ahead of Bitcoin on this. Not in Mastering Bitcoin ch. 1-5.

section: Keys and Addresses > Account = Hash(Kp) (lecture model)
prompt: In the lecture's model, how is an anonymous Bitcoin "account" linked to its owner, and how does the owner later claim the money?
choices: The account number is the one-way hash of a freshly generated public key, Account # = Hash(Kp); the owner claims funds by producing a signature with the matching secret key Ks, which anyone can verify with Kp.
The account number is the owner's email address; the owner claims funds with a password.
The account number is the private key itself; the owner claims funds by publishing it.
The account number is assigned by the miner who first pays the owner; claims require the miner's approval.
explanation: W4 s9 "Answering Q1 & Q2 Using Digital Signature": generate a random key pair (Kp, Ks); use the 1-way hash of the public key as the account number; claim money by signing with Ks; anyone verifies with Kp. Notes W4 s9 (B13). This is exactly the book's P2PKH address (HASH160 of the public key) and signature-based spending (ch04).

source.book: ch04 > Legacy Addresses for P2PKH; Public Key Cryptography
source.lecture: W4 s6, s9 +note (B13)

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation
prompt: What does a Bitcoin "wallet database" actually contain, according to the book?
choices: The bitcoins themselves, stored as encrypted coin files on the device.
Only keys; the bitcoins are records on the blockchain that those keys can spend.
A full copy of the blockchain, which is what makes it a wallet.
The user's identity documents and bank details, for compliance.
explanation: "Many people mistakenly believe that Bitcoin wallets contain bitcoins. In fact, what many people call a Bitcoin wallet--which we call a wallet database ...--contains only keys. Those keys are associated with bitcoins recorded on the blockchain."

source.lecture: W4 s12 +note (wallets in the ecosystem); W4 s29 +note ('Bitcoin doesn't tell you how much you have, but the transactions')

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation
prompt: What was the major drawback of early wallets that generated every key independently at random (nondeterministic wallets)?
choices: They could hold only a single bitcoin per key, so many keys were needed.
They needed an internet connection to sign, which leaked private keys.
A new backup was needed every time keys were generated, or funds could be lost.
Their keys were weaker than modern keys and easily brute-forced.
explanation: "All early Bitcoin wallet applications did this, but it required users to back up the wallet database each time they generated and distributed new keys ... Failure to back up the wallet database on time would lead to the user losing access to any funds received to keys that had not been backed up."

source.lecture: W4 s5, s9 +note (a new random key pair per received payment - the lecture's model is independent key generation)

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Deterministic Key Generation
prompt: What is the core idea of deterministic key generation?
choices: Each key is generated by a trusted server and delivered to the user.
The user picks keys from a list of words they find easy to remember.
Every key is derived from one random seed, so one backup covers all keys.
Keys are downloaded from the blockchain whenever they are needed.
explanation: A hash function turns "one random value ... into a practically unlimited number of seemingly random values" reproducibly. "A user of deterministic key generation can back up every key in their wallet by simply recording their seed and a reference to the deterministic algorithm they used."

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Public Child Key Derivation
prompt: The book shows that K + 123G == (k + 123)G. What does this make possible?
choices: Deriving the private key from the public key when the tweak is known.
Deriving child public keys from a parent public key with no private key.
Compressing the public key from 65 bytes down to 33 bytes.
Signing a transaction using only the public key and a tweak.
explanation: "It's possible to create child public keys even if you don't know anything about the parent private key. The value added to a public key is known as a key tweak." Bob can derive public children from Alice's public key; Alice adds the same tweaks to her private key to get the corresponding private children.

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Public Child Key Derivation
prompt: Which practical arrangement does public child key derivation enable, according to the book?
choices: A public-key-only frontend paired with a hardware signer that holds the private key.
Running a complete Bitcoin wallet without any private keys anywhere.
Letting miners generate fresh receiving addresses on behalf of users.
Storing private keys safely on a public web server behind an xpub.
explanation: "This technique is commonly used to separate wallet application frontends (which don't require private keys) from signing operations (which do require private keys)," e.g., a frontend distributes public keys and later gives the tweaks to a hardware signing device that derives the child private keys and signs.

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Hierarchical Deterministic (HD) Key Generation (BIP32)
prompt: What is a hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallet, and which standard defines it?
choices: Keys stored in a hierarchy of folders on disk, defined in BIP39.
A wallet governed by a hierarchy of company managers, defined in BIP44.
A tree of keys derived from one seed, defined in BIP32; the modern default.
Keys derived from the user's biometric data, defined in BIP21.
explanation: "Every modern Bitcoin wallet of which we're aware uses hierarchical deterministic (HD) key generation by default. This standard, defined in BIP32, uses deterministic key generation and optional public child key derivation with an algorithm that produces a tree of keys." BIP39 covers recovery words; BIP44 covers path structure.

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Seeds and Recovery Codes
prompt: Why is a wallet seed both powerful and dangerous?
choices: It doubles as the user's Bitcoin address, but it expires after a year.
It can mine blocks on its own, but doing so consumes electricity.
It is public information, but it can never be changed once created.
It regenerates every private key: recovery for the owner, total theft for a thief.
explanation: "If your wallet database is ever corrupted or lost, you can regenerate all of the private keys for your wallet using your original seed. But, if someone else gets your seed, they can also generate all of the private keys, allowing them to steal all of the bitcoins from a single-sig wallet."

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Seeds and Recovery Codes
prompt: What is the book's advice about relying on memory alone for a recovery code?
choices: Write it down anyway; memory alone risks loss, blocked inheritance, and coercion.
Memorize it and never write it down, because written copies get stolen.
Keep it only in a cloud password manager protected by a strong login.
Tell it to one trusted friend rather than writing it down anywhere.
explanation: "Most of the time, relying on memory alone is dangerous": forgotten codes lose funds forever, heirs can't recover, and attackers may coerce victims (Jameson Lopp documented over 100 physical attacks). The TIP: "we very strongly encourage you to consider writing it down."

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Seeds and Recovery Codes
prompt: Which recovery-code scheme splits a single seed across several codes so that, for example, any three of five codes can recover it?
choices: BIP39
SLIP39
Electrum v2
Aezeed
explanation: "SLIP39 allows a single seed to be distributed using multiple recovery codes that can be stored in different places (or by different people). When you create the recovery codes, you can specify how many will be required to recover the seed. For example, you create five recovery codes but only require three of them." Codex32 is a newer proposal with similar goals.

source.lecture: W2 s58-60, s97-98 +note (threshold signatures: t of n must collaborate) - a related idea, not SLIP39 itself

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Seeds and Recovery Codes
prompt: Which recovery-code scheme includes a "wallet birthday" and authenticates its optional passphrase so that a wrong passphrase produces an error?
choices: BIP39, used in most wallets.
SLIP39, the Shamir-split scheme.
Muun, the PDF-based scheme.
Aezeed, used in the LND wallet.
explanation: Aezeed "includes a wallet birthday in the recovery code, a reference to the date when the user created the wallet database," and "the Aezeed seed encryption scheme authenticates its optional passphrase and will return an error if you provide an incorrect value." BIP39, Electrum v2, and SLIP39 do not checksum the passphrase.

source.book: ch05 > Seeds and Recovery Codes; Recovery Code Passphrases

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Seeds and Recovery Codes
prompt: In BIP39, Electrum v2, and SLIP39, what is the consequence of the passphrase NOT being included in the checksum?
choices: The wallet rejects any passphrase whose words are not in its word list.
The passphrase is sent to the network so peers can verify it.
The passphrase can be recomputed from the recovery code alone.
Every passphrase yields a valid, different wallet: deniability but no error check.
explanation: "Three of the schemes (BIP39, Electrum v2, and SLIP39) do not include the optional passphrase in the checksum ... Every passphrase (including not using a passphrase) will result in producing a seed for a BIP32 tree of keys, but they won't be the same trees." Positive: decoy wallets and plausible deniability; negative: a mistyped passphrase silently yields an empty wallet.

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Backing Up Nonkey Data
prompt: Why can't wallet labels (e.g., "Paid Bob for podcast") be restored from a recovery code?
choices: Labels are encrypted with the recipient's key, which the owner lacks.
Labels are nondeterministic local data, not on the blockchain or in the seed.
Labels are kept by miners and deleted after six confirmations.
Labels are restored automatically; the book says nothing more is needed.
explanation: "Because address and transaction labels are stored only in each user's wallet database and because they aren't deterministic, they can't be restored by using just a recovery code." BIP329 proposes a standard export format for labels.

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Backing Up Nonkey Data
prompt: What solution do some wallets use to back up nonkey data (labels, Lightning channel state) safely on untrusted storage?
choices: Publishing the labels on the blockchain inside OP_RETURN outputs.
Emailing the unencrypted wallet file to the user's own address.
Frequent full wallet backups encrypted with a key derived from the seed.
Encoding the labels into extra words appended to the recovery code.
explanation: "One solution implemented by a few wallet applications is to frequently and automatically create complete backups of their wallet database encrypted by one of the keys derived from their seed ... This makes it safe to store the backup on untrusted computers such as cloud hosting services or even random network peers."

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths
prompt: Besides the recovery code, what else does the book say you must know to recover an HD wallet's funds?
choices: Nothing else; every other detail is recorded on the blockchain itself.
The seed algorithm (BIP39), the derivation algorithm (BIP32), and the paths used.
The IP address and peer list of the node the wallet originally used.
The block height and timestamp at which the wallet was first created.
explanation: Because a BIP32 tree has billions of possible keys at every level, "recovering from data loss requires knowing more than just the recovery code, the algorithm for obtaining your seed (e.g., BIP39), and the deterministic key derivation algorithm (e.g., BIP32)--it also requires knowing what paths in the tree of keys your wallet application used."

source.book: ch05 > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths
prompt: What does the book mean by "implicit paths"?
choices: Paths deliberately hidden from the user as a security measure.
Paths the wallet picks at random each time it is restarted.
Paths encoded inside the checksum bits of the recovery code.
Standard BIP-defined paths (e.g., BIP44/84/86) so users need not record them.
explanation: "Every time there's a change related to the addresses that wallet applications might want to generate, someone creates a BIP defining what key derivation path to use ... We call this solution implicit paths." The advantage is nothing extra to back up; the disadvantage is inflexibility.

source.book: ch05 > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths
prompt: Which BIP defines the derivation path for native segwit P2WPKH keys, and which for single-key taproot (P2TR)?
choices: BIP32 for P2WPKH and BIP39 for P2TR.
BIP44 for P2WPKH and BIP49 for P2TR.
BIP84 for P2WPKH and BIP86 for P2TR.
BIP16 for P2WPKH and BIP21 for P2TR.
explanation: The implicit-path table: BIP44 -> P2PKH (m/44'/0'/0'), BIP49 -> nested P2WPKH, BIP84 -> P2WPKH (m/84'/0'/0'), BIP86 -> P2TR single-key (m/86'/0'/0'). BIP32/39 define HD derivation and recovery words, not script-specific paths.

source.book: ch05 > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths

section: Wallet Recovery > Independent Key Generation > Backing Up Key Derivation Paths
prompt: What are "explicit paths," and what format do almost all wallets use for them?
choices: Writing the path on the same sheet as the words, which the book forbids.
Encoding the derivation path into the characters of each address.
Publishing the path on the blockchain so any wallet can find it.
Path and script info backed up with the code, almost always as descriptors.
explanation: "The second solution is to back up the path information with the recovery code ... We call this explicit paths ... Almost all wallet applications that use explicit paths as of this writing use the output script descriptors standard (called descriptors for short)." Example: sh(multi(2,022f...,03ac...)) is a P2SH 2-of-2 multisig descriptor.

prompt: Which three standards make up the wallet technology stack the book examines in detail?
choices: BIP16 script hashes, BIP21 payment URIs, and BIP9 version bits.
BIP39 recovery codes, BIP32 HD derivation, and BIP44-style implicit paths.
SLIP39 shares, Aezeed codes, and Codex32 hand-computable shares.
BIP173 bech32, BIP350 bech32m, and BIP329 label exports.
explanation: "We'll focus the rest of this chapter on the stack of technologies we think is most widely used in wallets as of early 2023: BIP39 recovery codes, BIP32 HD key derivation, BIP44-style implicit paths. All of these standards have been around since 2014 or earlier."

source.book: ch05 > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > BIP39 Recovery Codes
prompt: How does a BIP39 recovery code differ from a "brainwallet"?
choices: A recovery code is kept online; a brainwallet is kept on paper only.
The wallet generates recovery words at random; a brainwallet's words are user-chosen.
A recovery code has 4 words; a brainwallet has 12 or more words.
They are the same thing described under two different names.
explanation: "The primary difference is that a brainwallet consists of words chosen by the user, whereas recovery codes are created randomly by the wallet and presented to the user. This important difference makes recovery codes much more secure because humans are very poor sources of randomness."

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > BIP39 Recovery Codes
prompt: In BIP39, how is entropy turned into words?
choices: Entropy hashed with RIPEMD-160, its hex digits read off as word indexes.
Entropy + SHA256 checksum bits, split into 11-bit groups, mapped to 2,048 words.
Any 12 words the user types, hashed with SHA256 to make the seed.
Entropy split into 8-bit bytes, each mapped to one of 256 words.
explanation: The six generation steps: random sequence of 128-256 bits; checksum = first (entropy-length/32) bits of SHA256; append checksum; split into 11-bit segments; map each 11-bit value to one of 2,048 words; the sequence of words is the recovery code.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > BIP39 Recovery Codes
prompt: A BIP39 recovery code has 12 words. How much entropy does it encode, and how many words would 256 bits of entropy give?
choices: 256 bits; 256 bits would give 12 words too.
64 bits; 256 bits would give 48 words.
132 bits of pure entropy with no checksum; 256 bits gives 20 words.
128 bits of entropy (plus a 4-bit checksum); 256 bits of entropy gives 24 words.
explanation: The BIP39 table: 128 bits entropy + 4 checksum = 132 bits = 12 words; 160 + 5 = 15 words; 192 + 6 = 18; 224 + 7 = 21; 256 + 8 = 264 bits = 24 words. Most wallets in 2023 use 128 bits (12 words).

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > BIP39 Recovery Codes
prompt: How is the 512-bit seed derived from a BIP39 recovery code?
choices: A single SHA256 hash of the concatenated words, producing a 256-bit seed.
PBKDF2 with 2,048 rounds of HMAC-SHA512, salted with "mnemonic" + passphrase.
The words concatenated with spaces and used directly as the raw seed bytes.
AES-256 encryption of the words under the optional passphrase as the key.
explanation: Steps 7-9: PBKDF2 takes the recovery words and "a salt ... composed of the string constant 'mnemonic' concatenated with an optional user-supplied passphrase," and "stretches the recovery code and salt parameters using 2,048 rounds of hashing with the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm, producing a 512-bit value as its final output. That 512-bit value is the seed."

source.book: ch05 > From recovery code to seed

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > BIP39 Recovery Codes
prompt: Why does the book say most modern wallets use 128 bits of entropy (12 words) rather than 256?
choices: BIP32 cannot accept seeds derived from more than 128 bits of entropy.
Recovery codes longer than 12 words are prohibited in several countries.
A Bitcoin public key only offers ~128-bit security, so extra entropy adds little.
128 bits of entropy produces stronger private keys than 256 bits does.
explanation: "The security strength of a Bitcoin public key is 128 bits ... The implication of a security strength of 128 bits is that there's no apparent benefit to using more than 128 bits of entropy." The one extra benefit of longer codes: if an attacker sees half of a 256-bit code they still can't brute-force the rest. BIP32 accepts seeds of 128-512 bits.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Optional passphrase in BIP39
prompt: True or false: In BIP39 there is no such thing as a "wrong" passphrase; every passphrase leads to some wallet, which is empty unless it was previously used.
explanation: True. "There are no 'wrong' passphrases in BIP39. Every passphrase leads to some wallet, which unless previously used will be empty." The set of possible wallets (2^512) is far too large to guess or collide with.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Optional passphrase in BIP39
prompt: What two features does the optional BIP39 passphrase provide, and what risk does it introduce?
choices: Faster confirmations and lower fees; the risk is higher electricity use.
Legacy and taproot compatibility; the risk is a much longer address.
A second factor and a duress wallet; the risk is permanent loss if forgotten.
Blockchain encryption and miner anonymity; the risk is a hard fork.
explanation: The passphrase creates "a second factor (something memorized) that makes a recovery code useless on its own" and "a form of plausible deniability or 'duress wallet.'" Risks: "If the wallet owner is incapacitated or dead and no one else knows the passphrase, the seed is useless"; "if the owner backs up the passphrase in the same place as the seed, it defeats the purpose of a second factor."

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Creating an HD Wallet from the Seed
prompt: How does BIP32 create the master keys of an HD wallet from the root seed?
choices: The seed is used directly as the master private key, with no hashing.
The seed is base58check-encoded, and the result is the master xpub.
HMAC-SHA512 of the seed yields master private key m and master chain code c.
The seed is split into 12 equal pieces, one per first-level child key.
explanation: "The root seed is input into the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm and the resulting hash is used to create a master private key (m) and a master chain code (c). The master private key (m) then generates a corresponding master public key (M) using the normal elliptic curve multiplication process m x G."

source.book: ch05 > Creating an HD Wallet from the Seed

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Creating an HD Wallet from the Seed
prompt: Which three inputs does the BIP32 child key derivation (CKD) function combine, and how is its 512-bit output used?
choices: A password, a block hash, and a timestamp; the output is the child's address.
Two parent public keys and a nonce; the output is a Schnorr signature.
Parent key, chain code, and index; left half tweaks the key, right half is the new chain code.
The seed, the words, and the passphrase; the output is the account xpub.
explanation: "The child key derivation functions are based on a one-way hash function that combines: a parent private or public key, a seed called a chain code (256 bits), an index number (32 bits) ... The right-half 256 bits of the hash output become the chain code for the child. The left-half 256 bits of the hash are added to the parent private key to produce the child private key."

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Creating an HD Wallet from the Seed
prompt: What is the purpose of the chain code in HD key derivation?
choices: A record of the blockchain height at which the key was first created.
A link binding the wallet to one specific mining pool's payouts.
Extra entropy so a child key and index alone cannot reveal its siblings.
An encrypted copy of the user's passphrase for later verification.
explanation: "The chain code is used to introduce deterministic random data to the process, so that knowing the index and a child key is not sufficient to derive other child keys. Knowing a child key does not make it possible to find its siblings unless you also have the chain code."

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Extended keys / Public child key derivation
prompt: What is an "extended key," and what is the difference between an xprv and an xpub?
choices: Any key longer than 256 bits; xprv is for testnet and xpub for mainnet.
A key with an expiry date; the xprv expires before the matching xpub.
Key plus chain code; xprv derives private and public children, xpub only public.
A key stored in two locations; the xprv is the backup copy of the xpub.
explanation: "The two essential ingredients are the key and chain code, and combined these are called an extended key ... An extended private key is the combination of a private key and chain code and can be used to derive child private keys (and from them, child public keys). An extended public key is a public key and chain code, which can be used to create child public keys (public only)." Both are base58check-encoded with prefixes xprv/xpub.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Using an Extended Public Key on a Web Store
prompt: Gabriel loads an xpub onto his web store's payment server. What can the server do, and what can it not do?
choices: It can spend the store's funds automatically to pay suppliers.
It can reverse customer payments after they have confirmed.
It can produce exactly one address and must be reloaded per sale.
It can derive a fresh address per order but cannot spend anything.
explanation: "Gabriel can load an extended public key (xpub) on his website, which can be used to derive a unique address for every customer order ... Gabriel's website does not contain any private keys and therefore any hack of it can only steal the funds Gabriel would have received in the future, not any funds he received in the past."

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Extended keys / Public child key derivation
prompt: What is the "gap limit" of an HD wallet?
choices: The number of confirmations required before received funds can be spent.
The maximum size of a block, measured in weight units.
The target time between two consecutive blocks on the chain.
The most consecutive unused addresses a wallet will scan past before stopping.
explanation: Wallets generate a few keys at a time and extend as keys are used; keys handed out but never paid create gaps. "The maximum number of unused keys in a row that can fail to receive a payment without causing problems is called the gap limit." Exceeding it forces a wallet to refuse new addresses, generate beyond the gap (risking missed funds on restore), or reuse addresses.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Hardened child key derivation
prompt: What risk does hardened derivation protect against?
choices: A leaked child private key plus the xpub's chain code exposing siblings and parent.
An extended public key growing too long to fit inside a scannable QR code.
A child private key being derived with fewer than 256 bits of security.
Miners refusing to confirm transactions that originate from HD wallets.
explanation: "If a child private key is known, or somehow leaked, it can be used with the chain code to derive all the other child private keys ... Worse, the child private key together with a parent chain code can be used to deduce the parent private key. To counter this risk, HD wallets provide an alternative derivation function called hardened derivation."

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Hardened child key derivation
prompt: In HD wallet notation, what does an index written with a prime, such as 0' (or 0h), mean?
choices: A public key rather than the corresponding private key.
A key that belongs to the testnet chain rather than mainnet.
A hardened child; i' stands for index 2^31 + i.
The first key of a new account that has already been used.
explanation: "Index numbers between 0 and 2^31 - 1 are used only for normal derivation. Index numbers between 2^31 and 2^32 - 1 are used only for hardened derivation ... the first hardened child (index 0x80000000) is displayed as 0'. ... When you see an HD wallet index i', that means 2^31 + i." In ASCII the prime may be written as an apostrophe or the letter h.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > HD wallet key identifier (path)
prompt: In HD wallet path notation, what do "m" and "M" signify, and what does m/0'/0 describe?
choices: m = master private key, M = master public key; first normal child of the first hardened child.
m = mainnet, M = testnet; the first receiving address generated on the testnet chain.
m = mobile wallet, M = desktop wallet; the first key synchronized between the two devices.
m = mnemonic, M = master password; the first word of the recovery code, unhardened.
explanation: "Private keys derived from the master private key start with 'm.' Public keys derived from the master public key start with 'M.'" The path table: m/0'/0 = "the first normal grandchild private key from the first hardened child (m/0')." Ancestry is read right to left.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Navigating the HD wallet tree structure
prompt: What is the five-level structure defined by BIP44?
choices: m / wallet' / device' / user' / key / index
m / year' / month' / day' / hour / minute
m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index
m / network' / block' / transaction' / input / output
explanation: "BIP44 specifies the structure as consisting of five predefined tree levels: m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index." The first three levels use hardened derivation; the change level uses normal derivation so that xpubs can be exported for nonsecured environments.

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Navigating the HD wallet tree structure
prompt: What key does the BIP44 path M/44'/0'/0'/0/2 identify?
choices: The third change private key of the primary Bitcoin account.
The third receiving public key of the primary Bitcoin account.
The second receiving public key of the Litecoin account.
The first hardened key of the third account on testnet.
explanation: From the BIP44 example table: M (public branch), purpose 44', coin_type 0' (Bitcoin), account 0' (primary), change 0 (receiving), index 2 (third key) = "the third receiving public key for the primary Bitcoin account." Litecoin would be coin_type 2', testnet 1', and change addresses use 1 at the fourth level.

prompt: True or false: The book says data loss, rather than theft, may be the leading cause of lost bitcoins.
explanation: True. "One of the leading causes of lost bitcoins--perhaps the leading cause--is data loss. If the keys and other essential data required to spend your bitcoins is lost, those bitcoins will forever be unspendable. Nobody can get them back for you." section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail
prompt: Distinguish BIP32, BIP39, and BIP44 in one sentence each.
answer: BIP32 defines hierarchical deterministic key derivation (master key and chain code from a seed, normal/hardened child derivation, xprv/xpub). BIP39 defines recovery codes: turning 128-256 bits of entropy into 12-24 words and stretching them with PBKDF2 into a 512-bit seed. BIP44 defines the standard multi-account path structure m/44'/coin_type'/account'/change/address_index for organizing the BIP32 tree.
explanation: The three are often confused: derivation (32), words (39), paths (44).

source.book: ch05 > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail

section: Wallet Recovery > A Wallet Technology Stack in Detail > Hardened child key derivation
prompt: Explain why leaking an xpub together with one child private key can be catastrophic, and how hardened derivation prevents it.
answer: An xpub contains the parent public key and the chain code. With the chain code and any one child private key an attacker can compute the sibling private keys and even recover the parent private key, exposing the whole branch. Hardened derivation hashes the parent private key instead of the parent public key when creating the child chain code, so the chain code exposed in an xpub below a hardened level cannot be combined with a leaked child key to reach the parent or siblings; that is why level-1 children of the master key are hardened by convention.
explanation: Key points: xpub = pubkey + chain code; leaked child key + chain code -> siblings and parent; hardened uses parent private key; hardened levels sit above exported xpubs.

section: Wallet Recovery > One key per payment (lecture model vs book)
prompt: The lecture said a new random key pair is generated each time you receive a payment, so accounts are "created on the fly". How does this compare with the book's description of modern wallets?
choices: They contradict: the book says one address must be reused forever.

Both use a fresh key/address per payment; the lecture describes independently generated random keys, while the book says modern wallets derive each new key deterministically from one seed (BIP32 HD wallets), so a single recovery code backs them all up.
They are identical: both require a new recovery code for every payment.
The lecture's keys are public only; the book's keys are private only.
explanation: W4 s5 ("accounts are created on the fly when receiving a payment (= a random number!)") and W4 s9 ("Generate a random pair of public / secret keys") describe the whitepaper-style model of independent keys. Mastering Bitcoin ch05 explains that independently generated keys forced constant re-backups, so modern wallets use deterministic (HD) derivation from a seed while still giving every payment a new address.
